meta.blurb: Nina is almost ninety and still walks to the market every morning. Her granddaughter Elena, a data analyst, wants to know why. She follows the maps and numbers behind long lives, and sorts luck from place from choice.
meta.bible: Elena: a thirty-four-year-old data analyst, curious and careful with facts. Pavel: Nina's friend, eighty-eight, who still sells vegetables at a stall in the Market square. Nina: her grandmother, about to turn ninety, sharp, funny and active, who walks to the Market square every morning. Theo: Nina's six-year-old great-grandson. They live in Marlow, a small hill town. The story takes place in the weeks before Nina's ninetieth birthday party. Key terms: Life expectancy, Healthy life expectancy, Centenarian, Mediterranean diet, Sanitation, Vaccine, Heritability, Social ties, Purpose. The science is real and hedged: life expectancy is an average, not a limit; lists of countries change from year to year; findings about diet, alcohol, purpose and social life are mostly links and not proof; genes explain only part of the difference between people, with estimates that vary; no invented numbers, studies or quotes. Countries named are only those that often rank high in official life-expectancy tables. Voice: warm, curious, honest about luck and uncertainty. Nobody gets personal medical advice. Added in the full-length version: Iris is Nina's daughter and Elena's mother; Marek is Elena's older brother, an engineer, and Theo's father, so Theo is Elena's nephew and calls her Aunt Elena. Nina's card friends on Thursdays are Rosa, Tomas and Hana. Dr Quinn is the town doctor of Marlow, and a nurse at the clinic checks blood pressure. Karl is Pavel's cousin, who smoked all his life and lived to ninety-five, one lucky case. Pavel started at twelve on his father's cart, and his wife died eleven years ago. Nina's mother lived to eighty-eight; her father died at fifty-one in an accident at work. Nina left school at fourteen. Facts used: about thirty years of life expectancy around eighteen hundred and more than seventy now; John Snow and the cholera pump in London in 1854; smallpox declared wiped out in 1980; penicillin discovered in 1928 and widely used from the 1940s; Jeanne Calment of France died in 1997 aged one hundred and twenty-two; the World Health Organization advises at least one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity a week; adults need about seven to nine hours of sleep. Elena's five themes: move naturally, eat mostly plants, sleep enough, keep close people, have a reason to get up. Her toast: long life is partly luck, partly place and partly habit, and the aim is to add life to years and not only years to life. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

beats.scene: A cake with ninety candles beside a kitchen calendar and a framed family portrait
beats.summary: Nina is about to turn ninety, and her granddaughter Elena has come to help plan the party.

beats.scene: A steep hill town with crooked rooftops and a house with a blue door
beats.summary: Marlow is a small hill town of steep streets, and Nina has lived in the same house with the blue door for sixty years.

beats.scene: A small boy counting on his fingers beside a cake covered in candles
beats.summary: Theo, aged six, asks how many candles ninety will need and discovers that they cannot fit on one cake.

beats.scene: Elena sits at a laptop surrounded by charts, coffee and a tangle of cables
beats.summary: Elena works as a data analyst, turning large piles of numbers into plain answers.

beats.scene: Framed portraits of Nina's friends on a shelf, small candles beside them
beats.summary: Elena notices that many of Nina's friends from her youth are gone, while Nina herself is still active.

beats.scene: Nina pours tea at the table while Elena unfolds a world map
beats.summary: Over tea, Nina asks Elena why some people live much longer than others.

beats.scene: Elena counts three weeks on the calendar with a pencil
beats.summary: Elena offers to spend the three weeks before the party finding out what the evidence says.

beats.scene: Nina wags a finger at Elena across the kitchen table
beats.summary: Nina sets two rules: she wants what is true rather than what is fashionable, and no lectures.

beats.scene: A new notebook with three words written on its first page
beats.summary: Elena buys a notebook and writes three words on the first page: luck, place and habit.

beats.scene: Elena writes a promise at the top of a page by lamplight
beats.summary: Elena promises herself to use only careful sources and to say honestly when nobody knows.

beats.scene: Elena points to a newborn baby drawn at the start of a long arrow
beats.summary: Elena explains that life expectancy is the average number of years a newborn would live if today's death rates stayed the same.

beats.scene: Ten matchstick figures in a row, two of them very short
beats.summary: A small example shows how a few early deaths pull an average down.

beats.scene: A calendar with no date circled and a question mark above a person
beats.summary: Life expectancy describes a population and cannot predict how long any single person will live.

beats.scene: Nina holds up her hand like a pupil asking a question
beats.summary: Nina asks whether she has already outlived her expectancy, and Elena explains that survivors have further years ahead of them.

beats.scene: An arrow pointing from the past into a hazy future with small improvements marked
beats.summary: Life expectancy uses today's death rates, so people born now may live longer if conditions keep improving.

beats.scene: Theo pulls at Elena's sleeve beside a growth chart on the wall
beats.summary: Theo asks how long he will live, and Elena says nobody can say, though he can expect many years.

beats.scene: A curve climbing steeply on a chart, with an older couple beneath it
beats.summary: The risk of dying rises with age, roughly doubling about every eight years in adult life.

beats.scene: Two charts side by side, one with tall young bars, one with old
beats.summary: In rich countries today, most deaths happen at older ages, which was not true a century or two ago.

beats.scene: A staircase whose upper steps rise only slightly while lower steps climb sharply
beats.summary: The average has risen much more than the longest human lives, which seem to have a ceiling around one hundred and ten to one hundred and twenty years.

beats.scene: Elena writes a question in her notebook with an arrow pointing back in time
beats.summary: Nina decides that the real question is why the average rose so much, and Elena resolves to start with history.

beats.scene: A long staircase rising from the year eighteen hundred to today with small figures
beats.summary: Worldwide, life expectancy has risen from about thirty years around eighteen hundred to more than seventy today.

beats.scene: Babies and old people drawn beside a short bar and a long bar
beats.summary: The old averages were low mainly because many children died young, not because adults died at thirty.

beats.scene: Nina stands before a small framed portrait with an empty chair beside it
beats.summary: Nina remembers that, in her village when she was small, almost every family had lost a child.

beats.scene: A water pump with its handle removed and a crowd of people around it
beats.summary: In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in London to one water pump, an early proof that clean water saves lives.

beats.scene: Pipes under a street, a clean tap and a family washing their hands
beats.summary: Sewers, treated drinking water and handwashing greatly reduced diseases that once killed many children.

beats.scene: A child receiving a small injection from a smiling nurse
beats.summary: Vaccines protect against diseases such as polio and measles, and smallpox was wiped out in 1980.

beats.scene: A small glass dish with mould and a tablet of medicine beside it
beats.summary: Antibiotics, discovered in 1928 and widely used from the 1940s, made many infections treatable.

beats.scene: A farmer's field with full baskets and a well-fed child at a table
beats.summary: Better farming, storage and trade reduced famine, and better-fed children grew up stronger and healthier.

beats.scene: A mother and newborn in a clean hospital bed with a nurse nearby
beats.summary: Cleaner childbirth and better care for mothers and babies greatly cut deaths at birth and in the first year.

beats.scene: Elena draws a thick line from a drain to a long life
beats.summary: Elena concludes that the biggest gains in life expectancy came from public action more than from personal willpower.

beats.scene: A world map with some countries shaded light and others dark
beats.summary: Today a newborn in some countries can expect more than eighty-three years, and in others fewer than sixty.

beats.scene: Five small flags beside a long bar at the top of a chart
beats.summary: Japan, Switzerland, Spain, Italy, Singapore and Hong Kong often appear near the top of life-expectancy tables, though the lists change.

beats.scene: Nina holds a suitcase with a Spanish flag sticker and laughs
beats.summary: Nina jokes about moving to Spain, and Elena says that moving would not be a simple solution.

beats.scene: Two bars of very different heights with the word gap between them
beats.summary: The gap between the richest and poorest countries is more than twenty years, driven by infections, child deaths, conflict and poor access to care.

beats.scene: A climbing line on a chart with a steep rise marked between two years
beats.summary: Some places have gained decades of life expectancy within two generations, showing that large improvements are possible.

beats.scene: A line chart with a sudden dip and a slow recovery
beats.summary: Wars, epidemics and crises can cut life expectancy, as the COVID-19 pandemic did in many countries before it recovered.

beats.scene: A woman and a man side by side, a longer bar behind her
beats.summary: In almost every country women live longer than men, on average by about five years, for reasons that are not fully understood.

beats.scene: A tall bar with a short section coloured red at the top
beats.summary: Healthy life expectancy counts years lived in good health and is usually several years shorter than total life expectancy.

beats.scene: A crowd of people of many ages drawn as small different figures
beats.summary: Averages hide enormous variety, because within every country some people die very young and others live past one hundred.

beats.scene: Nina taps a notebook page where Elena has written a new aim
beats.summary: Nina says she wants years in good health, not just a bigger number, and Elena writes that down as the aim.

beats.scene: A graph with a steep curve that flattens, and coins stacked below
beats.summary: Richer countries tend to live longer, but the effect flattens: past a point more wealth adds little, and some middle-income countries do surprisingly well.

beats.scene: A school classroom, a clinic and a bus stop in a row
beats.summary: Countries that spend wisely on schools, clinics and basic services often reach long lives without being rich.

beats.scene: A city map with two neighbourhoods coloured differently along one train line
beats.summary: Within one city, life expectancy can differ by many years between neighbourhoods only a few stops apart.

beats.scene: A narrow flat with a damp wall beside a bright home with a garden
beats.summary: Differences between neighbourhoods come from income, jobs, housing, air, food and access to services, not only from personal choices.

beats.scene: A school desk with an open book beside a pair of reading glasses
beats.summary: Education is linked with longer life, probably because it leads to safer work, higher income and a better understanding of health.

beats.scene: A builder in a hard hat and an office worker, both tired
beats.summary: Work affects health: dangerous or exhausting jobs shorten lives, while long unemployment and constant insecurity are also linked with worse health.

beats.scene: A cold flat with frost on the window and a small electric heater
beats.summary: Warm, dry homes matter, because cold and damp housing is linked with more illness, especially in winter.

beats.scene: A balance with coins on one side and a crowd on the other
beats.summary: Some research links large gaps between rich and poor with worse health for everyone, but scientists still debate how strong that effect is.

beats.scene: A crossing with a green signal and a peaceful square with children playing
beats.summary: Safety matters too: fewer road accidents, less violence and peace all help more people reach old age.

beats.scene: Nina's blue door with a pension letter, a clinic sign and a timetable
beats.summary: Elena sees that Nina's own long life rests on a good place too: a pension, a nearby clinic, clean water and a safe town.

beats.scene: A birthday cake with a hundred candles on a table surrounded by smiling people
beats.summary: People who reach one hundred, called centenarians, are still rare, though their number has grown in many countries.

beats.scene: A group of elderly women laughing together on a bench
beats.summary: Most centenarians are women, and the oldest people in the world are mostly women too.

beats.scene: A French street with a very old woman in a chair holding a cane
beats.summary: Jeanne Calment of France, who died in 1997 aged 122, is the oldest person whose age has been verified.

beats.scene: A tiny group of very old figures at the top of a tall pyramid
beats.summary: People who live past one hundred and ten, called supercentenarians, are extremely rare.

beats.scene: Elena studies an old birth certificate with a magnifying glass at a desk
beats.summary: Elena checks Nina's birth certificate and learns how researchers verify very old ages by documents.

beats.scene: A village scene with a proud old man and a clerk holding a ledger
beats.summary: Where birth records are poor, claims of extreme old age are sometimes wrong, so researchers examine documents closely.

beats.scene: A line on a chart that bends and flattens at a very high age
beats.summary: Some studies suggest that after about one hundred and five the risk of dying stops rising, but other scientists disagree.

beats.scene: A small town with more elderly people than children on its streets
beats.summary: More people reach old age than before because of the gains of earlier chapters, so the number of very old people is growing.

beats.scene: A cigarette tin and a glass of wine beside a very old man's portrait
beats.summary: Some very old people smoked or drank heavily, a reminder that luck and genes matter and that the stories of survivors can mislead.

beats.scene: Nina waves her hand dismissively while Elena closes a heavy book
beats.summary: Nina says that she is not trying to reach one hundred and that she wants good days, so Elena turns to her daily habits.

beats.scene: Nina walks to the market square with a basket in the early morning
beats.summary: Elena rises early to follow Nina and sees that she walks to the market square every single morning.

beats.scene: Pavel behind a stall of tomatoes, beans and onions, weighing a bag
beats.summary: Nina buys vegetables from her friend Pavel, who is eighty-eight and has run his stall for decades.

beats.scene: Elena looks at a phone showing a step counter beside Nina's walking shoes
beats.summary: Elena's step counter shows that Nina walks several thousand steps before breakfast, more than Elena does in a working day.

beats.scene: A walking path up a hill, with small figures and a rising line
beats.summary: Many studies link more daily movement with a lower risk of early death, with the biggest gains for people who move from very little to a bit more.

beats.scene: A clock showing a week divided into small coloured blocks of walking
beats.summary: The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, which is about twenty minutes a day.

beats.scene: Nina carries a basket up steps and waters a row of tomato plants
beats.summary: Nina's life is full of small movements: stairs, gardening and carrying, which add up over a day.

beats.scene: Elena sits at a desk with a chair and a clock showing many hours
beats.summary: Long periods of sitting are linked with a higher risk of disease and early death, and breaking them up with short walks seems to help.

beats.scene: Pavel lifts a crate of apples onto his stall while Elena watches
beats.summary: Pavel lifts crates of vegetables all morning, which keeps his muscles working into old age.

beats.scene: Two friends walking and talking along a lane at an easy pace
beats.summary: A simple test of moderate effort is the talk test: you can talk but not sing, and walking with friends makes it easy to keep up.

beats.scene: Nina sits on the doorstep with her shoes off, looking pleased
beats.summary: Nina says she has never exercised in her life; her movement is part of living, which may be why she keeps it up.

beats.scene: A kitchen table with bean soup, bread and a jug of water
beats.summary: At lunch Nina serves bean soup, bread and vegetables, and Elena wonders how much the food explains.

beats.scene: Several different plates of food from different countries on one long table
beats.summary: There is no single longevity diet, but some eating patterns, such as the Mediterranean diet, are linked with lower risks of heart disease.

beats.scene: A table with beans, olive oil, vegetables, fish and bread in bowls
beats.summary: The Mediterranean pattern uses olive oil, nuts, fish and plenty of plants, and a large trial in Spain suggested it lowered heart problems.

beats.scene: A large bowl of lentils beside small bowls of meat and sweets
beats.summary: Many long-lived populations eat mostly plants and little processed meat or sugary drinks, though no one food is proven to be responsible.

beats.scene: Slices of whole-grain bread beside a jar of oats and a bowl of apples
beats.summary: Whole grains and fibre are linked with lower risks of heart disease and early death in large studies.

beats.scene: Sausages and a bottle of sugary drink beside a small warning sign
beats.summary: Health agencies advise limiting processed meat and sugary drinks, because both are linked with higher risks of illness.

beats.scene: A supermarket shelf of bright packets and a market table of plain food
beats.summary: Highly processed foods are linked with worse health in many studies, though it is hard to separate the food from the rest of a person's life.

beats.scene: A basket of fish and a bowl of nuts; Theo pulls a face
beats.summary: Fish and nuts are healthy parts of many diets, though Theo refuses the fish.

beats.scene: Four generations cooking together in a small kitchen
beats.summary: Cooking at home and eating together are habits that go with healthy eating, and Nina's kitchen is always busy.

beats.scene: Elena frowns at a stack of nutrition papers with question marks
beats.summary: Elena warns that nutrition research is difficult, because people report food poorly and most studies observe rather than test.

beats.scene: A plate with a little food left and a person smiling beside it
beats.summary: Nina stops eating before she is full, a habit some traditions recommend.

beats.scene: Mice, flies and a monkey beside a small plate of food
beats.summary: In animals, eating less sometimes extends life, but evidence in humans is unclear and the results in monkeys are mixed.

beats.scene: A kitchen scale beside a tape measure and a bowl of fruit
beats.summary: A healthy weight is linked with lower risks of diabetes and heart disease, but weight is only one part of health.

beats.scene: A slow tortoise passing a speeding hare on a path of small steps
beats.summary: Slow, gradual changes in habits tend to last longer than crash diets, according to many studies.

beats.scene: A glass of wine with a question mark and a stopped clock behind it
beats.summary: People once thought moderate drinking was protective, but newer research doubts it, and many experts now say no level of alcohol is clearly good for health.

beats.scene: A cigarette crossed out beside a calendar with years added
beats.summary: Tobacco is one of the largest causes of early death, so people who smoke less tend to live longer.

beats.scene: A salt shaker beside a blood pressure gauge
beats.summary: A lot of salt is linked with higher blood pressure, and many countries advise limiting it.

beats.scene: Two cups, one of tea and one of coffee, beside a window
beats.summary: Large studies have not found harm from moderate amounts of tea or coffee for most adults, and some find a small benefit.

beats.scene: A slice of birthday cake on a plate with a lit candle
beats.summary: One slice of cake is not the problem; what matters is the whole pattern of eating over years.

beats.scene: A page of three short lines about food under a heading
beats.summary: Elena sums up the table: mostly real food, mostly plants and not too much.

beats.scene: A bed with a deep blue blanket under a window with a crescent moon
beats.summary: Adults need about seven to nine hours of sleep, and regularly sleeping much less is linked with poorer health.

beats.scene: A tired brain with a small night lamp and sleeping figures beside it
beats.summary: Sleep is when the body repairs itself and the brain sorts memories, and short sleep is linked with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.

beats.scene: A clock in the middle of the night above a very long sleeper
beats.summary: Sleeping far more than nine hours is also linked with poorer health, probably because illness often causes it, though this is uncertain.

beats.scene: Nina sleeps in an armchair with a hat over her eyes
beats.summary: Nina takes a short rest after lunch every day, and research on naps is mixed but short ones seem harmless for most people.

beats.scene: A pot on the boil with steam and a person holding their head
beats.summary: Short bursts of stress are normal, but chronic stress harms health, raising blood pressure and affecting sleep and mood.

beats.scene: A teapot, a prayer mat and a hammock around a quiet courtyard
beats.summary: Many cultures have daily habits of rest, prayer, tea or quiet, which may help people to unwind.

beats.scene: Theo in pyjamas being tucked into bed beneath a dim lamp
beats.summary: Regular routines, a dark and quiet room and fewer screens before bed are common advice for sleeping well, and Theo's bedtime shows how they work.

beats.scene: Sunrise over a made bed with a clock at six
beats.summary: Nina wakes at the same hour every day, and regular times for waking and eating seem to support healthy sleep.

beats.scene: Nina's quiet garden bench with a cup of tea and an empty chair
beats.summary: Nina says she tries not to worry too much, and while worry cannot always be switched off, calm habits and good company help.

beats.scene: Elena counts three small icons: a bed, a sun and a tea cup
beats.summary: Elena sums up the chapter: enough sleep, a little rest and calm routines help, but they are not a guarantee.

beats.scene: Four older friends playing cards around a kitchen table
beats.summary: On Thursday afternoon Nina's friends Rosa, Tomas and Hana arrive to play cards and argue happily.

beats.scene: A thick report with a bar chart of two groups of people
beats.summary: A review of nearly 150 studies found that people with stronger social relationships had a better chance of survival over time.

beats.scene: One person alone in a crowded room, another reading in a quiet one
beats.summary: Loneliness, the feeling of lacking company, is different from living alone, and both are linked with health in different ways.

beats.scene: A neighbour knocks on a door with a pot of soup
beats.summary: Friends and family may help health by giving practical help, noticing illness, offering encouragement and easing stress.

beats.scene: An arrow going both ways between a smiling couple and a doctor's bag
beats.summary: Healthier people also find it easier to make and keep friends, so the link between friendship and health probably goes in both directions.

beats.scene: Three generations at a long table, with a great-grandson passing a bowl
beats.summary: Nina lives close to her family, and being part of a family or community gives older people care and a feeling of being useful.

beats.scene: Elena alone at a city window with a phone showing a missed call
beats.summary: Elena admits that she lives alone in the city, sees her friends rarely and often lets calls go unanswered.

beats.scene: Pavel knocks at Nina's window with a bag of apples early in the morning
beats.summary: Pavel checks on Nina when she does not appear at the market, which shows how neighbours notice when someone is missing.

beats.scene: A library notice board with posters for clubs and classes
beats.summary: Making new friends later in life is not easy, but clubs, classes, volunteering and libraries all offer ways to meet people.

beats.scene: Elena writes the words keep close people with a small drawing of two cups
beats.summary: Elena adds keep close people to her list of themes, and Rosa says that you lose count of the years but not of the friends.

beats.scene: A person rising from bed as the sun rises behind a window
beats.summary: Elena asks Nina what makes her get up, and Nina answers that her garden, family and opinions need her.

beats.scene: A graph with two lines, one rising from a small sun
beats.summary: Studies link a strong sense of purpose with a lower risk of early death, though it is hard to be sure which comes first.

beats.scene: Pavel hands a bag to a customer under a striped awning
beats.summary: Pavel never stopped working at his stall, and says that he will stop only when his customers stop being rude to him.

beats.scene: Nina reads a storybook aloud to Theo on the sofa
beats.summary: Nina reads to Theo and helps him with his letters, and giving help to others keeps older people active and connected.

beats.scene: A community hall with people singing and sharing food together
beats.summary: Regular community gatherings, religious or not, are linked in some studies with longer life, mostly through support and routine.

beats.scene: An old stone church and a mosque and a temple standing side by side
beats.summary: In some studies, people who attend religious services regularly live longer, perhaps because of community and routine, and the effect does not depend on belief alone.

beats.scene: A choir, a dance circle and a drum group with big smiles
beats.summary: Group activities like singing, dancing and playing music may help well-being, mood and connection, although the evidence on long life is limited.

beats.scene: Nina holds a tablet with her great-grandson's face on its screen
beats.summary: Nina keeps learning new things, such as video calls, and learning something new keeps people curious and engaged.

beats.scene: A woman in an old coat laughs on a park bench
beats.summary: Some studies find that people with a positive view of ageing live longer, but it is hard to know whether attitude is the cause.

beats.scene: Elena writes a reason to get up, with a small sun above
beats.summary: Elena adds a fifth theme, have a reason to get up, though she notes that losing purpose after retirement or loss is hard and calls for support.

beats.scene: A small town with shops, a school and a clinic close together
beats.summary: In Marlow, shops, services and friends are within walking distance, which builds daily movement and contact into life.

beats.scene: A grey city street with traffic smoke beside a clear green park
beats.summary: Air pollution is linked with heart and lung disease and earlier death, and the World Health Organization estimates that it contributes to millions of early deaths a year.

beats.scene: A park with tall trees, a pond and people on benches
beats.summary: Living near parks and green spaces is linked with better health, perhaps because they encourage movement, calm and company, though proof is difficult.

beats.scene: A cycle path beside a safe road with a tram and children on bikes
beats.summary: Cities that make walking, cycling and public transport safe and easy tend to build movement into daily life.

beats.scene: A crossing with a green signal and children and an older man crossing
beats.summary: Safe crossings, calm traffic and low crime make people willing to go out, especially older people.

beats.scene: A snug house with thick walls and a well-lit window on a snowy night
beats.summary: A well-built, warm and well-lit home also protects older people from falls and cold.

beats.scene: Nina climbing a steep Marlow street with a basket, smiling at the view
beats.summary: Marlow's steep hills give Nina a daily workout without any planning.

beats.scene: A market stall of fresh fruit beside a counter selling fast food
beats.summary: What food is easy to reach shapes what people eat, so shops and markets selling fresh food nearby support healthier eating.

beats.scene: A bench with a handrail, a public toilet sign and a long crossing signal
beats.summary: Age-friendly towns provide benches, public toilets and longer crossing times, so older people can go out comfortably.

beats.scene: Elena draws a map of Marlow with small helpful icons on it
beats.summary: Elena concludes that place works quietly, and good habits become easier when the streets support them.

beats.scene: A nurse takes the blood pressure of an older man at a clinic
beats.summary: At Marlow's clinic Elena watches a nurse measure an older man's blood pressure and learns that good health care prevents many early deaths.

beats.scene: A gauge of blood pressure with a gentle arrow and a pill organiser
beats.summary: High blood pressure is a leading risk factor for early death, often has no symptoms, and can be checked cheaply and treated.

beats.scene: A row of older people wearing coats waiting in a clinic hallway
beats.summary: Vaccines for older people, such as those against influenza, protect against serious illness, and recommendations differ by country.

beats.scene: A woman with a calendar of check-ups and a small marker beside each
beats.summary: Screening tests can find some illnesses early, but their benefits and limits vary, so people should discuss which are right for them with a doctor.

beats.scene: A line chart of heart deaths falling over many decades
beats.summary: Deaths from heart disease have fallen in many rich countries, partly through better treatment and partly through prevention.

beats.scene: A table with several small bottles and a pharmacist's list
beats.summary: Many older people take several medicines, and doctors advise reviewing them regularly, a matter for each person's own doctor.

beats.scene: An older woman lifts a light weight while standing near a chair with support
beats.summary: Strength and balance exercises reduce falls, a leading cause of injury in older people, and they are useful at any age.

beats.scene: A pair of glasses and a hearing aid on a tidy table
beats.summary: Regular checks of eyesight and hearing help older people stay connected and safe, since poor hearing and sight can lead to withdrawal.

beats.scene: Two figures on opposite sides of a river with a bridge missing between them
beats.summary: Not everyone can reach a clinic, because cost, distance and long waits get in the way, and countries differ in how they share care.

beats.scene: Dr Quinn at a desk with a patient chair and a big open book
beats.summary: Dr Quinn tells Elena that a book cannot say what is right for an individual, so Elena writes a note to ask your own doctor.

beats.scene: An old wooden cart with a faded sign and a boy of twelve
beats.summary: Pavel tells Elena that he began selling vegetables from his father's cart when he was twelve.

beats.scene: Pavel's day drawn as a clock: waking at five, loading a cart, selling, resting
beats.summary: Pavel wakes at five, loads his cart, sells until two and rests in the afternoon, a regular rhythm he has kept for decades.

beats.scene: Customers of different ages crowd around Pavel's stall and chat
beats.summary: Pavel knows every customer by name, and the stall keeps him in daily contact with many people of every age.

beats.scene: Pavel holds a framed portrait of a woman with a kind smile
beats.summary: Pavel's wife died eleven years ago, and he says that his friends, his stall and Nina helped him through his grief.

beats.scene: Pavel winks while holding a very large turnip like a trophy
beats.summary: Pavel jokes that he is old but not finished, and he treats his age with humour and without fear.

beats.scene: A magnifying glass over the words attitude to ageing beside a smiling elder
beats.summary: Research suggests that older people with positive views of ageing recover better from illness, though more research is needed.

beats.scene: Pavel rubs a stiff knee while sitting on a crate
beats.summary: Pavel has a bad knee and some other ailments, which shows that a long life is not always a perfect one.

beats.scene: An older man sits on a stool and weighs fruit for a small girl
beats.summary: Part-time work and being useful help older people remain active and connected, and Pavel is proud that people still depend on him.

beats.scene: Pavel and Nina eat sandwiches on a bench in the Market square
beats.summary: Pavel and Nina eat lunch together on a bench, unhurried, and they take time to talk and watch the world go by.

beats.scene: A single thread woven into a many-coloured cloth

beats.scene: Elena at her desk with a laptop and a half-eaten sandwich late at night

beats.scene: A sandwich in a plastic box, and a long table with a hot meal

beats.scene: A phone glowing beside a bed at one in the morning

beats.scene: A single walking shoe by a front door with a clock at lunchtime

beats.scene: Theo looks up at Elena with big eyes beside a birthday card

B1B2: In three weeks Nina will turn ninety, and the whole family is planning a big party in the hill town of Marlow. Her granddaughter Elena has come for Sunday lunch to help with the guest list.
Marlow is a small town built on a steep hill, with narrow streets and a market square at the top. Nina has lived in the same house with the blue door for more than sixty years.

Nina's great-grandson Theo is six years old, and he wants to know how many candles a cake for ninety will need. He counts to thirty on his fingers, gives up, and decides that the cake will have to be as big as a table.
Elena is thirty-four, and she works as a data analyst, which means she turns large piles of numbers into plain answers. She cannot hear a surprising claim without wanting to check where it came from.

On the shelf there are photographs of Nina's school friends, and most of them are no longer alive. Elena realises that she has never asked why her grandmother is still so active when so many others are not.
Over a pot of tea, Nina asks her granddaughter why some people live so much longer than others. Elena admits that she does not know the whole answer, but she thinks that the evidence is interesting.

Elena offers to use the three weeks before the party to find out what the research really says. Nina laughs and says that three weeks is not a long time, but that at her age she is used to short deadlines.
Nina has two rules for the project, and she explains them firmly. She wants to hear what is true rather than what is fashionable, and she does not want to be told how to live.

That evening Elena buys a thick notebook at the corner shop and writes three words on the first page: luck, place and habit. She does not know yet how the three will fit together, but they seem a fair way to sort what she finds.

Before she sleeps, Elena makes a promise to herself: she will use only careful sources, and she will say honestly when nobody knows. A book about long life, she decides, should not promise more than the evidence can give.
Elena begins with the words, because many people misunderstand them. Life expectancy is the number of years a newborn would live if today's death rates stayed the same throughout life.
To show how an average works, Elena draws ten people on a page. If eight live to eighty and two die as babies, the average is much lower than eighty, even though most lived long lives.
Nobody lives exactly as long as the average, Elena says, because the number describes a whole population. It cannot tell anyone when their own life will end, and it was never meant to.
Nina asks whether she has already outlived her life expectancy. Elena explains that anyone who has survived to old age has avoided many dangers, so her own expected years are higher.
The calculation freezes today's death rates and applies them to a newborn. In real life, rates have usually kept falling, so children born today may well live longer than the figure suggests.
Theo has been listening, and he asks how long he will live. Elena smiles and tells him that nobody can say, but that a boy born in his country today can expect many, many years.

In adult life, the chance of dying in any given year rises with age, and it roughly doubles about every eight years. This is a pattern seen in many countries, though the exact figures vary from place to place.
In rich countries today, most people die in old age. Two hundred years ago, a much larger share of deaths happened to babies, children and young adults.

Averages have risen a great deal, but the longest human lives have risen much less. Scientists still debate whether there is a fixed ceiling, though very few people have ever passed one hundred and ten.

Nina sums up the lesson in her own words: the real question is why the average rose so much, and who stays above it. Elena agrees and decides to begin with history, because the largest changes happened there.
Around the year eighteen hundred, average life expectancy across the world was about thirty years. Today it is more than seventy, which is one of the biggest improvements in human history.

Elena explains that the old averages were low mainly because so many babies and young children died. It does not mean that adults dropped dead at thirty, because many people lived into their sixties and seventies.

Nina remembers her own childhood in a village where almost every family had lost a child. Sickness that doctors can treat today was a danger that people simply expected, and she says she is glad Theo will not know it.

In London in 1854, a doctor named John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to a single water pump. When the handle was removed, the cases fell, and the link between dirty water and disease became hard to deny.
Over the next century, towns built sewers and treated their drinking water with chlorine, and people learned to wash their hands. These changes cut the diseases that once killed so many children.

Vaccines trained the body to resist diseases such as polio and measles, which once crippled and killed many children. Smallpox, which had killed people for thousands of years, was declared wiped out in 1980.

In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould could kill bacteria, and by the 1940s penicillin was being used widely. Infections that had once been deadly, such as some kinds of pneumonia, became much easier to treat.
Better farming, storage and transport meant that fewer places suffered from famine. Children who were well fed grew up healthier and were better able to fight off infection.

Childbirth also became much safer, thanks to cleanliness, trained midwives and doctors, and better care for newborns. In rich countries today nearly all babies survive their first year, which was never true in the past.

Elena looks at her notes and sees a pattern: most of the rise came from things that whole societies did together. Clean water, vaccines and medicine did more than anyone's willpower, and Nina nods in agreement.
Elena spreads a world map on the table and shades the countries by life expectancy. In some, a newborn can expect to live more than eighty-three years, while in others the figure is below sixty.

Japan, Switzerland, Spain, Italy, Singapore and Hong Kong often appear near the top of the official tables. The lists change from year to year, however, and different sources rank the places differently.
Nina jokes that she should move to Spain at once. Elena replies that it is not so simple, because people carry their past with them, and a country's average says little about one new arrival.
The gap between the countries with the longest and shortest lives is more than twenty years. The causes include infections, child deaths, conflict, hunger and the lack of good health care.
Some places have added decades to their life expectancy in only two generations. That shows that large improvements are possible when governments, doctors and families all work in the same direction.

Progress is not always steady, because wars, epidemics and crises can push life expectancy down. The COVID-19 pandemic lowered it in many countries in 2020 and 2021, and it later recovered in many places.

In nearly every country, women live longer than men, by about five years on average. The reasons are not fully understood, but they probably include biology, smoking, risky work and how often people see doctors.

Elena introduces another idea, healthy life expectancy, which counts only the years lived in good health. It is usually several years shorter than total life expectancy, because many people spend their last years with illness.
Elena reminds her grandmother that each country's number is only an average. Within every country, some people die young and some live past one hundred, and the differences between people are huge.
Nina says that she is not interested in a bigger number for its own sake. She wants years in good health, so Elena writes that down as the real aim of the whole project.
Elena shows that, on average, richer countries have longer lives. The curve flattens at the top, however, so extra wealth adds little, and some middle-income countries do better than expected.
Countries that spend carefully on schools, clinics and basic services can do well even if they are not rich. Simple things, such as nurses in every village, can save a great many lives.
Elena finds a study of a city where life expectancy changes along a single train line. People in neighbourhoods only a few stops apart can differ by many years in how long they live.

These differences come from many things at once, including income, jobs, housing, air quality, and access to shops and clinics. They cannot be explained by personal choices alone, because people do not choose all of these for themselves.
In many countries, people with more years of education tend to live longer. The reasons probably include safer jobs, better income and an easier understanding of health information.

Work affects health in more than one way, and not always as people expect. Dangerous or exhausting jobs can shorten lives, and long periods without work, or constant insecurity about money, are also linked with worse health.
Housing also matters, although it is easy to overlook when people talk about health. Cold, damp homes are linked with more illness in winter, so heating and repairs are part of the story.

Some researchers believe that societies with very large gaps between rich and poor have worse health overall. Other scientists disagree about how strong the effect is, so Elena records it as a debate and not a fact.

Safety matters too, because fewer road accidents, less violence and peaceful conditions all help more people reach old age. In many countries, simple steps such as seat belts and speed limits have saved a great many lives.

Elena looks again at her grandmother's life and sees how much of it rests on place. Nina has a pension, a clinic within walking distance, clean water and a safe town, and these are not things that everyone has.
A person who reaches one hundred is called a centenarian. They are still rare, but their numbers have been growing in many countries for decades.
Most centenarians are women, and the oldest people in the world are mostly women too. This is partly the same difference that gives women longer lives at every age.

The oldest person whose age has been checked carefully was Jeanne Calment of France, who died in 1997 at the age of one hundred and twenty-two. Nobody since has come close to her record, so she remains an extreme exception.
People who live past one hundred and ten are called supercentenarians, and they are extremely rare. In any country, only a handful of people have ever reached such an age.

To see how researchers check an age, Elena finds Nina's birth certificate in a drawer and studies it carefully. It shows the date, the place and the signature of a witness, and it matches the family's story exactly.

Where birth records were poor or missing, some claims of extreme old age have turned out to be mistaken. Researchers therefore check documents closely, and many famous claims have not survived their examination.
