Nina grew quiet and said that she remembered her childhood village very well, a place where almost every family had lost a child at some time. Illnesses that a doctor treats in an afternoon today were dangers that people simply expected and bore, she said, and nobody thought of it as a scandal. She added, looking at Theo, that she was deeply glad that he would never have to know such fear.

Elena told the story of John Snow, a London doctor who in 1854 mapped the homes of people struck by cholera and found that they clustered around a single water pump. When the handle of the pump was removed, the outbreak faded, and the connection between dirty water and deadly disease became very hard to ignore. It was one of the first great victories of public health, and it was won with a map and a careful mind.

Over the following century, towns and cities built sewers, treated their drinking water with chlorine and taught their citizens to wash their hands, and the effect was dramatic. Diarrhoea, typhoid and cholera, which had once killed children in vast numbers, retreated in the places where clean water and sanitation arrived. Elena pointed out that nobody notices a tap that works, which is exactly why the achievement is so easy to forget.

Vaccines, Elena said, work by training the body to recognise an enemy before it ever meets it, and they have spared countless children from polio, measles and other cruel diseases. The most striking victory was over smallpox, which had afflicted humanity for thousands of years and was declared eradicated in 1980 after a long worldwide campaign. Nina remembered standing in line at school for her own turn and thinking only that the needle was far too big.

In 1928 the scientist Alexander Fleming noticed that a mould growing in a forgotten dish had killed the bacteria around it, and by the 1940s penicillin had become a medicine that saved lives across the world. Infections that had once been a death sentence, from infected wounds to certain kinds of pneumonia, became curable in a matter of days. Elena added that bacteria are now learning to resist these drugs, which is a serious worry for the future.

Farming improved steadily too, with better tools, better seeds and better ways of storing and moving food, and fewer regions fell victim to famine as a result. Children who were properly fed grew taller and stronger, and they were far better equipped to survive the infections that came their way. Hunger, Elena observed, is a hidden cause of many deaths that never appear on a certificate with its own name.

Childbirth, once among the most dangerous events in a woman's life, became far safer thanks to cleanliness, trained midwives and doctors, and better care for newborn babies. In rich countries today nearly all infants live through their first year, a thing that no earlier generation could have counted on, and this alone accounts for a very large part of the rise in the average. Elena said that she had checked the figure three times because it still seemed too good to be true.

Elena read through her notes and saw an unmistakable pattern, which was that most of the great rise in life expectancy had come from things that whole societies did together, and not from the efforts of individuals. Clean water, vaccines, medicine and food had done more for the average life than any amount of personal willpower could have done. Nina nodded slowly, and said that this was worth remembering the next time somebody blamed an old woman for her own illness.

Elena spread her map across the table and shaded each country according to its life expectancy, and the pattern that emerged was startling. In some places a newborn can expect to live for more than eighty-three years, whereas in others the figure is below sixty, which means a gap of a whole generation between babies born on the same day. Nina traced the darkest regions with her finger and said nothing for a while.

Japan, Switzerland, Spain, Italy, Singapore and Hong Kong, Elena said, are among the places that often appear near the top of the official tables of life expectancy. The ranking shifts from year to year and from one source to another, so nobody should treat it as a race with a permanent winner, and the differences between neighbours at the top are small. What matters is not who stands first but how many different countries manage to reach such high numbers.

Nina announced with a twinkle that she would pack her suitcase at once and move to Spain, for the sake of science. Elena replied that it was not so simple, because a country's average is made by the way its people live over a whole lifetime and says very little about a new arrival at ninety. Besides, she added, her grandmother would miss her tomatoes and her card friends far too much.

The distance between the countries with the longest and shortest lives, Elena explained, is more than twenty years, and it is not a matter of mystery. Infectious diseases, the deaths of small children, conflict, hunger and the absence of good health care all weigh heavily on the places where life is shortest. The causes are well known, she added, and many of them can be treated, which is the hopeful part of the story.

The map, however, was not fixed in stone, and Elena showed her grandmother several countries whose lines had climbed steeply in the space of two generations. In some places, people gained twenty or thirty years of life expectancy in a single lifetime, which proves that the gap can narrow quickly when governments, doctors and families pull in the same direction. The bars on the chart are a report on the past and not a sentence on the future.

Progress, she cautioned, does not always move in a straight line, because wars, famines and epidemics can all push life expectancy sharply downward. The COVID-19 pandemic lowered it in many countries during 2020 and 2021, including some wealthy ones, though it has since recovered in many places. Nina recalled the quiet streets of Marlow in those months and the empty chairs at Thursday cards.

In almost every country in the world, Elena reported, women live longer than men, by about five years on average, and the pattern has held for a very long time. Researchers have not settled on a single explanation, but they suspect a mixture of biology, differences in smoking and drinking, dangerous work and the willingness to visit a doctor. Nina observed that she had been saying so for decades, mostly at men's expense.

Elena then introduced a second concept, healthy life expectancy, which counts only the years that people live in good health and leaves out the years spent in serious illness or disability. It is usually several years shorter than the total, since many people spend their final years living with long-term conditions. The distinction matters, she said, because what most people want is not just more years but more good ones.

Elena was careful to remind her grandmother that every number on the map is an average, and that averages hide enormous variety. Inside every country some people die far too young and others pass one hundred, and the spread of lives around the middle is far wider than the gap between neighbouring countries. If she wanted to understand Nina's long life, she said, she would have to look not at maps alone but at a single human being.

Nina tapped the page with a bony finger and said that she was not interested in a large number for its own sake, since a long life that is spent in a hospital bed is not much of a prize. What she wanted, and what she suspected everyone wanted, was a long stretch of years in which she could walk, think and laugh with her friends. Elena wrote it down at the top of the page as the true aim of the project.

When Elena plotted income against life expectancy, the points formed a steep curve that rose quickly at first and then flattened out. Among poorer countries, more money tends to mean far longer lives, she said, but beyond a certain level extra wealth adds very little, and some middle-income countries achieve surprisingly good results through sensible public health. How a country spends its money, she concluded, matters as much as how much it has.

Some countries with modest incomes achieve long lives, Elena found, because they invest carefully in the plain, unglamorous things such as primary schools, village clinics, clean water and vaccination. A nurse in every village, she said, can save more lives than a hospital in a distant capital. It is a reminder that the best returns in health are often found in the cheapest and most ordinary places.

Elena found a study that mapped life expectancy along a single railway line in a big city, and the result was almost unbelievable. Every few stops, the average life of the people living near the station dropped or rose by a year or more, so that passengers on one short ride could cross a gap of many years. The difference lay not in the carriage but in the neighbourhoods around each station.

The gaps between neighbourhoods arise from many causes working together, Elena explained, among them income, the kind of work people do, the quality of their homes, the air they breathe and the shops and clinics within reach. It would be unfair and inaccurate to blame them all on personal choices, since few people choose their parents, their schools or the street where they were born. Place, in other words, is something that happens to us long before it becomes something we decide.

In country after country, Elena discovered, people with more years of schooling tend to live longer than those with fewer. The most likely explanation is a chain of small advantages, which includes safer work, steadier income, a better grasp of health information and more confidence in dealing with doctors. Nina, who had left school at fourteen and read every book in Marlow's library afterwards, said that she hoped the evidence would not insult the self-taught.

Work, Elena noted, shapes health in more than one direction, and not always in the way that people expect. Dangerous or physically exhausting jobs can shorten lives, but so too can long periods of unemployment and the constant strain of not knowing whether the money will last, both of which are linked with poorer health in many studies. A good job, she concluded, is one that is safe, reasonably secure and fairly paid, and it is a kind of medicine that no pharmacy can sell.

Housing, it turned out, has a quiet influence on the length of life, because cold and damp homes are linked with more breathing problems and more illness, particularly in winter and among older people. Heating, insulation and simple repairs therefore belong in the story of long life, even though they rarely appear in magazine articles about longevity. Nina said that her own house had been drafty for sixty years, and that she had never forgiven the windows.

A few researchers argue that societies with very large gaps between rich and poor have worse health overall, even among the comfortable, perhaps because of stress and mistrust. Other scientists doubt that the effect is large, or that it is caused by inequality itself, and the arguments are still unsettled. Elena put the idea in her notebook under the heading of open questions, which was a heading she suspected would grow.

Safety, Elena found, plays a larger part than most people imagine, since fewer road accidents, less violence and long periods of peace allow many more people to reach old age. In many countries plain measures such as seat belts, speed limits and safer crossings have saved a great many lives, and none of them required anybody to change their personal habits. Nina observed that her own generation had known war, and that peace was perhaps the most underrated health policy of all.

Elena looked again at her grandmother's life and saw how much of it rested on the quiet help of place, which she had never counted before. Nina had a pension, a clinic within walking distance, clean water from her tap and a town where it was safe to walk at dusk, and these were advantages that millions of people of her age did not have. It was not the whole explanation, but it made her explanation of Nina's long life a good deal more humble than it had been that morning.

Elena introduced a word that sounded grander than it was, which was centenarian, meaning a person who has lived to one hundred or more. Such people are still rare in any population, but their numbers have been growing steadily in many countries for several decades. When Theo heard the word he repeated it six times, and by the end of the afternoon it was his favourite.

Among centenarians, Elena found, women outnumber men by a wide margin, and the very oldest people in the world are mostly women. This is partly the same difference that gives women a longer average life at every age, though it is stronger at the extreme end of the scale. Nina remarked dryly that she had always suspected the men of giving up too early.

The oldest person whose age has been verified with great care, Elena said, was a Frenchwoman named Jeanne Calment, who died in 1997 at the age of one hundred and twenty-two. Nobody since has come within several years of her record, which suggests that she was an extreme exception and not a sign of things to come. Nina looked at her own hands and said that she would settle for a good deal less.

Beyond the centenarians, Elena explained, lies an even smaller group called supercentenarians, who have lived past the age of one hundred and ten. They are extraordinarily rare, and in most countries only a handful of people have ever reached such an age with documents to prove it. At that height of the pyramid the air is thin, and the evidence thinner.

To understand how researchers verify great ages, Elena fetched Nina's birth certificate from a drawer, where it had lain folded among old recipes for many decades. It recorded the date, the place and the signature of a witness, and it matched the family's story exactly, which is the standard that serious investigators demand. A claim of extreme age is only as strong as the paper that supports it, she said.

In places where birth records were poor or missing, Elena warned, some famous claims of extreme old age have turned out to be mistaken, through error, pride or the wish to claim a pension. Researchers therefore examine census records, baptism registers and old letters with the patience of detectives, and many celebrated cases have collapsed under their scrutiny. A wonderful story, she remarked, is not the same thing as a verified one.

A few studies of the very oldest people suggest that after about one hundred and five the yearly risk of dying stops climbing and levels off, which would mean that there is no fixed wall at the end of life. Other scientists dispute the finding, pointing to the small numbers and the uncertain records, and the question remains unsettled. Elena wrote it in her notebook with a question mark, and found that the question mark was beginning to feel like an old friend.

The number of very old people is growing, Elena realised, largely because the gains of the last century are now showing up at the far end of life. Children who were protected by clean water and vaccines in the twentieth century have grown into old men and women, and the crowd at the top of the age ladder has thickened. Nina said that it felt like being a pioneer, though it mostly felt like being tired.

Elena noticed with some discomfort that a handful of very old people had smoked or drunk heavily for decades and still lived past ninety. These cases, she said, remind us that luck and genes play a large part, and that the colourful stories of survivors can mislead us if we forget the many people who did not survive to tell theirs. She underlined the word luck in her notebook and promised herself to come back to it.

Nina laughed, waved a hand and declared that she was not trying to reach one hundred, only to have a good day tomorrow and another the day after. Elena closed the heavy book with a thump and agreed that the numbers and the records could wait, since a better laboratory was sitting in front of her. She decided that she would begin, quite literally, at the beginning of her grandmother's day.

At seven o'clock, Elena stumbled out of the blue door behind her grandmother and into the cool light of the morning. Nina strode up the steep street to the Market square with a basket on her arm, nodding to the baker and the postman as she went, exactly as she had done on thousands of mornings before. Elena, panting a little, realised that she was already being outpaced by a woman of ninety.

In the Market square, Nina stopped at the stall of her old friend Pavel, a stooping, cheerful man of eighty-eight who had been selling vegetables there for more than sixty years. They exchanged insults about each other's age, the price of tomatoes and the state of the weather, and the conversation was clearly one that had been going on for decades. Elena realised that she was watching a ritual and not just a purchase, and that the ritual probably did Nina a great deal of good.

When Elena checked the step counter on her phone, it showed that her grandmother had already walked several thousand steps before nine o'clock in the morning. On an ordinary working day in the city, Elena admitted, she did fewer than that between waking and sleeping, and most of those were from the bed to the desk. It was an uncomfortable discovery, and she wrote it down in her notebook without any comment, which was the kindest thing she could do for herself.

Elena turned to the research and found that many large studies link more daily movement with a lower risk of early death. The biggest gain appears when someone who does almost nothing starts to do a little, and the benefit seems to level off at higher amounts, so that nobody needs to become an athlete. These studies show a link, she reminded herself, and healthier people may also simply find it easier to move.

The World Health Organization, Elena read, advises adults to do at least one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity every week, which works out at a little over twenty minutes a day. Brisk walking counts as moderate activity, and so do cycling, gardening and dancing, so the target is much more modest than most people fear. Nina said that she had never spent twenty consecutive minutes sitting still in her life, except at funerals.

Back at the blue house, Elena counted that her grandmother climbed the steep stairs at least a dozen times a day, and spent an hour or more in the little garden digging, watering and carrying pots. None of this counted as exercise in Nina's mind, but it added up to far more movement than Elena managed on the days when she dutifully visited the gym. Movement, she realised, can be woven into a life like thread into cloth, and it is then almost impossible to pull out.

Researchers have also found that long hours of sitting are linked with a higher risk of heart disease and early death, even among people who exercise regularly at other times. Breaking up the sitting with short walks and stretches appears to help, although the exact amounts are still being studied. Elena glanced guiltily at her chair and was glad that it was in another town.

Elena watched as Pavel hoisted crate after crate of apples and onions from his little cart onto the stall, without a grunt and without hurrying. Lifting and carrying are a kind of strength training, she realised, and Pavel had been doing it six days a week since before her mother was born. His shoulders, Elena thought, were those of a man thirty years younger, and he carried them with quiet pride.

Elena came across a simple rule for judging effort, called the talk test, which says that moderate activity is the kind during which you can still hold a conversation but could not sing a song. She tried it on the way home with her grandmother, who passed with ease and then confessed that she did not talk to herself either, because she had no time. It was a pleasant way to learn that company and exercise work well together.

That evening Nina declared on the doorstep that she had never exercised in her entire life, and that she had simply lived. Elena thought that this might be the real lesson, because movement that belongs to ordinary life, such as shopping, gardening and visiting, is far easier to keep up than a special effort squeezed into a busy week. She underlined the first of her five themes, which she would later call move naturally.

For lunch Nina ladled out a thick bean soup with warm bread and a plate of vegetables fresh from Pavel's stall, and Elena ate two helpings with great pleasure. Between mouthfuls she wondered aloud how much of her grandmother's long life could be credited to the cooking, and how much to the cook. Nina replied that soup was soup and that nobody had ever lived longer by overthinking it.

There is no single longevity diet, Elena told her grandmother, and people in different parts of the world have lived long on quite different foods. Even so, patterns of eating that are rich in vegetables, beans, whole grains, fruit and fish, such as the traditional Mediterranean diet, are linked with a lower risk of heart disease and some other illnesses. The pattern matters more than any individual ingredient, she said, and it is the pattern that most families can actually change.

The traditional Mediterranean pattern, Elena explained, relies on olive oil, nuts, fish and a great abundance of plants, with only small amounts of red meat and sweets. A large trial in Spain suggested that people who followed it, with extra olive oil or nuts, had fewer heart attacks and strokes, although some experts criticised the way the study was run. Science rarely delivers a perfect result, she added, and it usually delivers a useful one.

In many places where people live long, Elena found, the traditional diet is made mostly of plants, with little processed meat and few sugary drinks. Mostly plants does not mean only plants, and many of these populations eat modest amounts of fish, dairy or meat, but research cannot prove that any single food is the reason for their long lives. People who eat this way usually live differently in many other respects too, which makes the evidence hard to read.

Whole grains and dietary fibre are among the few foods with a consistent record in large studies, which link them with a lower risk of heart disease, diabetes and early death. Brown bread, oats, beans and lentils are everyday examples, and they have the added merit of being cheap, filling and easy to cook. The most boring advice in nutrition, Elena remarked, is often the most reliable, and the least likely to appear on a magazine cover.

Health agencies around the world advise people to limit processed meats such as bacon and sausages, and to cut down on sugary drinks, since both are linked with a higher risk of illness. The warning concerns habits over many years and not the occasional treat, and nobody is suggesting that a single birthday sausage is a catastrophe. Nina said that she was greatly relieved, because she had been planning to eat several at the party and had not wanted to feel guilty.

Many studies link highly processed foods, such as packaged snacks, ready meals and fast food, with a greater risk of illness. It is difficult, Elena cautioned, to separate the effect of the food itself from everything else in a person's life, such as income, time and stress, and researchers are still trying to untangle the evidence. For now, she said, the simple rule of eating food that looks like food seems wise without being proven.

Fish and nuts, Elena reported, belong to many of the healthiest eating patterns in the world, and she suggested that they appear on the table more often. Theo pushed his plate away from the fish with great dignity and announced that he would eat the bread and nothing else. Nina observed that preferences are formed early, and that even a six-year-old can be a stubborn expert on his own tastes.

Elena also noticed that her grandmother cooked nearly everything herself and almost never ate alone, which are habits that tend to go along with healthier eating. It is hard to say which of these things matters most, since eating together brings company, time and routine, but it is clear that a kitchen full of people tends to be a healthier place than a drive-through window. The food on the table, she realised, is only one part of the meal, and perhaps not even the most important part.

Elena added a warning to her notebook, which was that nutrition research is genuinely difficult. People remember their meals poorly, most studies merely observe what people choose to eat rather than testing it, and the effects of any one food are small and slow. Be suspicious, she wrote, of anything described as a superfood, since there is no such thing as a single ingredient that rescues a whole life.

At the end of the meal Nina put down her fork while there was still a little soup in her bowl, and she folded her napkin with satisfaction. Her mother had always told her to stop eating before she felt completely full, she said, and the habit had stayed with her for eighty years. Several traditions around the world have similar sayings, and Elena wondered whether they were wise or only old.

In laboratory experiments with worms, flies and mice, animals fed a carefully reduced diet have often lived longer than those who ate freely. In humans the evidence is unclear, and the two long studies on monkeys gave mixed results, so Elena marked the idea as interesting but unproven. Nobody, she added, should interpret this as advice to go hungry, since starving is not the same as eating a little less.

Research links a healthy body weight with lower risks of diabetes, heart disease and some cancers, and Elena presented the evidence with all the gentleness she could manage. However, weight is only one part of health, and a single number cannot describe how well any particular person is living. Fitness, sleep, friendships and mood all have their say, and Nina said that she had known thin people who were miserable.

Elena's reading suggested that slow and gradual changes in habits tend to last much longer than crash diets, which most people abandon within months. People who change one small thing at a time, such as an extra walk or a smaller portion, are far more likely to be doing it a year later than those who try to reform their whole lives overnight. Nina remarked that she had never seen a revolution that began on a Monday and lasted.

For years, headlines announced that a glass of wine a day was good for the heart, and many people were glad to believe it. Newer research has cast doubt on the claim, partly because some of the non-drinkers in older studies were ill or former drinkers, and many experts now say that no amount of alcohol is clearly good for health. Nina raised her teacup in salute to the science, and said that she preferred tea anyway.

Of all the findings that Elena had collected, the clearest and the least controversial concerned tobacco, which is one of the largest single causes of early death in the world. Countries where fewer people smoke tend to enjoy longer lives, and individuals who never smoke avoid a great many diseases of the heart, lungs and blood vessels. Here, at least, she said, there was no need to hedge or hold back.

Elena also read that a diet high in salt is linked with higher blood pressure, which in turn raises the risk of heart disease and strokes. Many health bodies therefore advise people to limit salt, much of which comes not from the salt shaker but from bread, sauces and packaged food. Nina looked at the loaf on the table with some suspicion and then cut herself another slice.

Nina was relieved to learn that large studies have found no harm in moderate amounts of tea or coffee for most adults, and some have even hinted at a small benefit. The evidence is not strong enough to recommend that anybody drink more, and some people react badly to caffeine, but it does allow a grandmother to enjoy her morning cup in peace. Elena noted that many habits seem to gain their health benefits from the company that comes with them.

Nina cut herself a small slice of cake and ate it with obvious enjoyment and no guilt whatsoever, and Elena had no wish to stop her. A single slice is not the problem, she agreed, because what shapes health is the pattern of eating over many years and not the content of any one afternoon. Food that is enjoyed slowly and in good company, she added, rarely does anyone much harm, whatever its calorie count.

Elena summed up what she had learned about the table in three short lines, and as she wrote them she realised how closely they matched the lunch that she had just eaten. Mostly real food, mostly plants and not too much, she wrote, and then added a fourth line to remind herself that none of it was a cure or a promise. Nina read the page over her shoulder and said that it sounded exactly like her mother.

Elena turned next to sleep, and discovered that most adults appear to need about seven to nine hours each night. Regularly sleeping much less is linked with poorer health and, in several studies, with a higher risk of early death, although some people do seem to manage on a little less. It is a fact that is hard to enjoy, she admitted, when you are writing at midnight.

During sleep, researchers believe, the body carries out repairs and the brain sorts the memories of the day, although the details are still being studied. People who regularly sleep too little show higher rates of heart disease, diabetes and low mood, and tired people also make more mistakes and more accidents. A good night's sleep, Elena decided, is one of the cheapest forms of medicine.

The studies also show a curious pattern at the other extreme, which is that people who regularly sleep far more than nine hours have poorer health on average. Scientists suspect that illness or depression may be causing the long sleep and not the other way round, though the matter is not settled. It was a good example, Elena said, of why a link in the data does not always point in the direction we expect.

After lunch each day, Nina sank into her armchair, tipped a straw hat over her eyes and slept soundly for about twenty minutes. Research on afternoon naps is mixed, with some studies finding benefits and others finding none, but short naps seem harmless for most people and are certainly pleasant. Elena crept out of the room and wrote in her notebook that the evidence was inconclusive, then fell asleep on the sofa.

A short burst of stress is a normal part of life, and it can even help a person to meet a deadline or to react in an emergency. Stress that never lets up, however, can raise blood pressure, spoil sleep and darken the mood, and over many years it takes a real toll on the body. Elena, whose own deadlines had never lifted, found this paragraph hard to write with a straight face.

Elena noticed that many cultures have built a daily pause into their way of life, whether it is prayer, a long midday rest, an afternoon tea or an evening sit on the doorstep. Such habits may help people unwind and lower the body's level of stress, although their effect is hard to measure and they cannot be separated from the rest of a culture. Nina's own pause, she realised, was her tea at four o'clock, taken in a particular chair and never rushed, whatever else was happening.

Theo's bedtime was a model of method, Elena observed, with a bath, a story and a dim lamp at the same hour every evening. Sleep experts often recommend exactly this kind of routine for adults as well as children, along with a quiet, dark room and fewer screens in the hour before bed. The advice that works for six-year-olds, she thought ruefully, might work for thirty-four-year-olds too.

Nina woke at six o'clock every morning without an alarm clock, and had done so for as long as anybody could remember. Regular times for waking, eating and going to bed appear to help the body keep a steady daily rhythm, which is one reason why shift workers often struggle, though Nina simply said that she liked the mornings. Elena, who needed three alarms and a stern threat to leave her bed, listened with equal parts admiration and envy.

Nina remarked that she tried not to worry too much, and then admitted with a smile that this was easier said than done. Worry cannot always be switched off by willpower, Elena pointed out, and it would be unkind to suggest that anxious people simply need to relax, but calm routines, good company and professional help can make a real difference. She added gently that anyone who is struggling with worry should speak to a doctor, because that is a medical matter and not a failing.

Elena closed the chapter on rest with a short summary, which said that enough sleep, a little quiet time and calm routines all seem to help, but that none of them is a guarantee. She felt rather pleased with herself for having stopped before midnight, and promised herself, with only moderate confidence, that she would try to follow her own notes. The next question, she decided, concerned the people who surrounded Nina, and who might be doing as much for her as the soup.

On Thursday afternoon, three of Nina's oldest friends, Rosa, Tomas and Hana, arrived to play cards, drink coffee and argue happily about the rules. They had been meeting every week for more than thirty years, and in all that time nobody had ever agreed on how the game was supposed to be played. Elena sat in the corner with her notebook and tried to look as if she were not part of the evidence.

Elena had found a famous review that combined the results of nearly one hundred and fifty studies, and it reported that people with stronger social relationships had a better chance of surviving over the following years. The researchers compared them with people who were lonely or isolated, and the difference was comparable in size to some well-known health risks. The studies observed people and did not experiment on them, she added, so the evidence shows a strong link and not a proven cause.

Elena was careful to explain that loneliness is a feeling of lacking the company one wants, and that it is not the same thing as living alone or being alone. Some people live by themselves and feel perfectly content, while others feel desperately lonely in a crowded house, and researchers treat these as separate conditions with different effects on health. Rosa, who lived alone and was never lonely, said that she would like it in writing.

Researchers have suggested several ways in which friends and family might protect health, and Elena listed them for the card players. Friends give practical help, notice when something seems wrong, encourage good habits, offer comfort in hard times and make life feel less stressful, and all of these may add up over decades. Tomas said that he could confirm the first one, because Nina had once nursed him through a very serious cold.

Elena added the usual warning, which was that the link between friendship and health probably runs in both directions. People who feel well find it easier to go out and to keep up friendships, so it is hard to say how much of the benefit comes from friends and how much from good health. Researchers try to correct for this, she said, but they cannot do it perfectly.

Nina lived only ten minutes from her daughter Iris and her grandson Marek, and every Sunday the family crowded round the long table in her kitchen. Elena watched Theo carry the bread to his great-grandmother, solemn as a priest, and saw how much it pleased her to be needed. Being part of a family, she wrote, brings older people not only care and company but also the feeling of being useful.

Writing about friendship made Elena uncomfortable, because she lived alone in a flat in the city and saw her own friends only a few times a month. She often let calls go unanswered because she was tired after work, promising herself that she would ring back at the weekend, and the weekend usually vanished. It was a small thing, she told herself, but the notebook seemed to be asking her to look at it.

Nina told Elena that the previous winter she had missed one morning at the market because of a heavy cold, and within an hour Pavel was knocking at her window with a bag of apples. Neighbours who notice when somebody has gone missing can make a real difference to older people, she said, especially to those who live alone and have nobody to call. She said it without any sign of surprise, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world.

Elena also considered the harder case of those who have no Thursday card game, since making new friends later in life is not always easy and not everyone has a lifetime of friendships behind them. Clubs, classes, choirs, volunteering and local libraries all offer ways to meet people, and many towns have groups that welcome newcomers with open arms. The first visit is the hardest, she wrote, which is true of most good things.

Elena added a new line to her list of themes, which read keep close people, and underlined it twice. Rosa, who was looking over her shoulder, said that after eighty one loses count of the years, but never of the friends, and then she demanded that somebody deal the cards. The game began again at once, with the noise of a family and the rules of nobody.

Elena asked her grandmother what it was that made her get up so promptly every morning, and Nina answered without hesitation. She had a garden to tend, a family to feed and a great many opinions that needed to be shared, and every one of them required her attention before breakfast. It was an answer that no questionnaire could have anticipated, and it was entirely convincing.

Several large studies have linked a strong sense of purpose in life with a lower risk of early death, even after taking account of age, income and other illnesses. It is hard to be sure which comes first, since people who feel well may find purpose easier to hold, and those who feel purposeless may also be unwell. Elena wrote the finding down in her notebook as likely but not proven, which was becoming a very familiar phrase.

Pavel, when Elena asked him about retirement, snorted with laughter and said that he had never really done it and did not intend to. He would stop selling vegetables, he said, on the day that he stopped enjoying it, and for the moment his customers would be lost without him, just as he would be lost without them. His stall was clearly a workplace and a social club at once, with the best gossip in Marlow.

On Sunday afternoons, Nina sat on the sofa with Theo against her side, reading him stories and helping him sound out his first words, and neither of them wished the hour to end. Looking after children, volunteering and helping neighbours all give older people a reason to stay active and connected, and the benefit appears to flow in both directions. Theo, for his part, claimed that he was really the one doing the teaching, and he had the confidence to prove it.

On Sunday mornings, Nina joined a group of neighbours in the town hall to sing, and afterwards everybody stayed for tea and cake and a long exchange of news. Regular community gatherings of this kind, whether religious or not, have been linked in some studies with longer life, probably through the support, routine and sense of belonging that they provide. Nina's voice, Elena noted, was strong, accurate and perfectly happy to be heard, rising above the choir like a sparrow in the rafters.

Some studies have found that people who regularly attend religious services tend to live longer, in several different faiths and countries. Researchers suspect that the community, the routine and the practical support may account for much of this, though some people also find that faith itself helps them to face hardship, and science has no business judging anyone's beliefs. Elena treated the subject with the respect that it deserved and the caution that it needed.

Singing, dancing and playing music in groups seem to lift the mood and create a feeling of connection, and in some studies they have been linked with better well-being in later life. The evidence that they lengthen life is limited, Elena admitted, but the evidence that they make days more enjoyable is much stronger. A longer life with no joy in it, she wrote, is hardly a bargain.

Nina had recently learned to use a tablet for video calls, a skill she acquired with Theo's patient help and a good deal of muttering. Learning new things keeps people curious and engaged, and it can leave older people feeling capable rather than left behind, which is a feeling that cannot be measured but is easy to see. Her cousin in another country, she reported with triumph, now got a call every week.

In one set of studies, people who held a positive view of growing old were found to live longer, on average, than those who feared it, even after accounting for their health at the start. It is hard to know, however, whether the attitude is a cause or merely a symptom of feeling well, and Elena was cautious about turning the finding into advice. Nina, who found old age hilarious, said that it did not need a study.

Elena added a new theme to her list and wrote have a reason to get up, drawing a small sun above the words. She also wrote a note to herself that purpose is not always easy to find after retirement or after the loss of someone dear, and that it is not a character flaw to need help in finding it. Her grandmother, she decided, was not only lucky but occupied, with a life full of small jobs that nobody else could do.

Elena walked the length of Marlow with a notebook and a stopwatch, and she was struck by how close everything lay. The baker, the school, the clinic, the library and the pharmacy were all within a few minutes' walk of the Market square, so that errands became exercise and exercise became conversation without anybody noticing. A town built on this scale, she realised, does part of the work on behalf of its people.

Elena turned to the air, and found that air pollution is linked with heart disease, lung disease and earlier death in a very large body of research. The World Health Organization estimates that it contributes to millions of early deaths every year around the world, most of them in places where dirty fuels are burned indoors or traffic is heavy. Nina looked up at the clear sky over Marlow and said that she had never thought of air as a luxury.

Studies in several countries link living near parks, trees and green spaces with better health and, in some cases, longer lives. The reasons might include more walking, cooler air, less noise and more chances to meet neighbours, although it is difficult to separate the benefit of greenery from the other advantages of the leafy parts of town. Elena decided that proof could wait, since a bench under a tree needs no research.

Some cities have deliberately made walking, cycling and public transport safe and pleasant, with wide pavements, protected cycle lanes and frequent trams or buses. People in these places tend to build movement into their ordinary days without having to think about it, which is exactly what the best public health policy would hope for. Nina said that she had always thought that town planners ought to be doctors.

Safe crossings, slow traffic, good lighting and low crime all make people more willing to leave their homes on foot, and this matters most of all to older people. Someone who feels afraid in the street will probably stay indoors, Elena observed, and an old person who stays indoors loses movement, company and sunlight all at once. A safe street, she wrote, is a kind of medicine that the whole town takes together.

A warm, well-lit and well-built home, Elena found, protects older people from the cold and from the falls that are one of the most common causes of serious injury in later life. Good lighting, handrails, level floors and sturdy stairs may sound dull, but they prevent a great many accidents and allow older people to remain independent for longer. Nina's house, with its steep stairs and its single handrail, had clearly been in the business of keeping her fit.

Marlow stood on a steep hill, and Nina climbed it several times a day without a second thought, with her basket on one arm and her stick unused on the other. The geography of the town gave her a daily workout for which she never had to pay a membership fee or remember a timetable. Elena, puffing at her side, observed that the hills were the town's gift to its oldest inhabitants and its revenge on its youngest.

Another quiet influence on health, Elena discovered, is the food that is easy to reach, because people tend to eat what is close at hand. Where shops and markets selling fresh food are nearby, healthier eating comes more easily, and where there is only fast food on every corner it becomes much harder, whatever people intend. Pavel's stall, she reflected, was a small public health service in a striped awning.

Some towns have set out deliberately to become friendly to older people, installing benches at regular intervals, public toilets, smooth pavements and crossing signals that allow enough time to cross. These simple things make it easier and safer for older residents to go out and stay in touch, and they cost very little compared with the problems that they prevent. Elena noticed that Marlow had a bench every hundred steps and decided that a kind person had planned it.

Elena drew a map of Marlow in her notebook and marked every place that helped its people to move, to meet one another and to breathe good air. She concluded that place works quietly in the background of every life, and that good habits are far easier to keep when the streets, the shops and the services support them instead of working against them. It was not a rule, but it was a very good reason to care about town halls.

At the small clinic in Marlow, Elena sat in a corner and watched a nurse strap a cuff around an elderly man's arm and read the number with a practised eye. Good health care, she learned, prevents many early deaths through vaccines, screening and the treatment of problems before they become emergencies. The clinic, with its worn chairs and its patient, cheerful staff, was one of the town's less visible monuments.

High blood pressure, the nurse explained, is one of the leading risk factors for early death in the world, and it frequently causes no symptoms at all until it has done damage. A simple, cheap check can discover it, and once it is found it can usually be treated with changes in daily habits or with medicine, which is why regular checks matter. Elena was careful to note that anyone with questions should take them to their own doctor.

Vaccines are not only for children, the nurse reminded her, and some of them protect older adults from serious illness, with influenza being a well-known example. National health services recommend different vaccines at different ages, and the right choices depend on each person's health and history, so these are matters for a doctor and not for a notebook. Elena wrote that down in her notebook with a firm line underneath it, because it seemed the most important sentence of the day.

Screening tests, the nurse said, can discover some illnesses early, sometimes before a person has felt any symptoms, and this can lead to treatment that works better. Their benefits and limits vary from test to test and from person to person, and some may find things that would never have caused trouble, so the sensible question is always which tests are right for you. That question, Elena noted carefully, can only be answered by a person's own doctor, who knows their history and their other medicines.

In many rich countries, Elena read, deaths from heart disease have fallen sharply over the last several decades, even as the number of older people has grown. Researchers believe that both better treatment, such as improved care after a heart attack, and better prevention, such as less smoking and better control of blood pressure, have played a part. The credit, she observed, is shared between the hospitals and the living rooms of the nation, and between the researchers and the patients who listened.

Many older people take several medicines every day, the nurse said, and it is a good idea for doctors to review them regularly to make sure that they still fit together and still do their jobs. This is a matter for each person's own doctor and pharmacist, and nobody should ever stop or change a medicine on the strength of something they have read in a book. Elena noted, with some alarm, that her own grandmother kept hers in an old biscuit tin on the kitchen shelf, next to the tea.

Falls are one of the leading causes of injury in older people, the nurse explained, and trials have found that exercises for strength and balance can reduce the number of falls. They are useful at any age, whether practised in a class, at home or on the way to the market, and people with health conditions should check with their doctor before beginning. Nina promptly demonstrated standing on one leg, wobbled a little against the table, and then declared that the lesson was complete and that it was time for tea.

The nurse also encouraged people to have their eyesight and hearing checked regularly, because poor sight and hearing can make an older person withdraw from company and become more isolated. Glasses and hearing aids are small devices with large consequences, helping people to read, to cross roads safely and to follow a conversation at the card table. Tomas, who had recently been fitted with a hearing aid, said that he could now hear all the insults.

Elena remembered, however, that not everyone has a clinic within a few minutes' walk, and that cost, distance and long waiting times keep many people away from care that they need. Countries differ greatly in how they share the cost and the services among their people, and these differences are among the reasons that their life expectancy differs. Nina said that a good clinic was worth more to a town than a fine statue.

Elena ended her visit with a short conversation with Dr Quinn, the town doctor, who told her gently that no book, however carefully researched, can say what is right for any particular person. Individuals differ in their history, their medicines and their risks, and only someone who knows them can give advice that fits. Elena wrote a note in the margin of the page, which said ask your own doctor about your own health.

Pavel told Elena that he had started selling vegetables from his father's wooden cart at the age of twelve, standing on a box so that he could see over the scales. He had remained in the Market square ever since, apart from a few difficult years during the war, and he knew every cobblestone by heart. He said it all with the casual pride of a man whose life has had one clear shape.

Pavel's day, he explained, began at five o'clock in the morning, when he loaded his cart in the dark and wheeled it to the Market square before the town had woken. He sold until two in the afternoon and then went home for a long rest, a steady rhythm that he had kept for decades and that gave his days a shape as dependable as a clock. He had not a single complaint about any of it, and he said that a man with a steady routine has no time to feel sorry for himself.

Pavel, Elena noticed, knew the name of every customer who came to the stall, and he asked after their children, their knees and their gardens as he weighed the onions. In the course of a single morning he spoke to dozens of people of every age, and each of those conversations was a small thread in the web of a town. He was, in his way, a one-man centre of social contact, and the town would have felt it keenly if he had ever stayed at home.

Pavel showed Elena a framed photograph of his wife, who had died eleven years earlier, and he said that he still missed her every day. His friends, his stall and especially Nina had helped him through that terrible time, he said, and he did not believe that he would have managed alone. Grief affects health, Elena knew, and the support of other people is one of the things that soften its effects.

Pavel announced, with a large turnip raised like a trophy, that he was old but not finished, and then he roared with laughter at his own joke. He treated his age with humour and without fear, Elena noticed, and he teased himself more than he teased anybody else. The turnips, he said, had taught him patience, and he commended the lesson to anybody who had a spare month.

Some research suggests that older people who hold a positive view of ageing recover better from illness and disability than those who see old age as a decline, although more studies are needed. Elena wrote that a good attitude is probably helpful and certainly pleasant, but that it cannot prevent illness, and that nobody should be blamed for being unwell. Nobody, she insisted, loses a battle against disease because of a lack of cheerfulness.

Pavel had a bad knee, a little trouble with his hearing and a few other small ailments, and he made no attempt to hide any of them. His story showed Elena that a long life is not necessarily a perfectly healthy one, and that many people live well and fully with long-term conditions. She added a note to her page, which said that years in good health are not the only years that matter.

Pavel was proud that people still depended on him, a pride that was neither loud nor vain but simply a quiet satisfaction in being useful. Part-time work, volunteering and helping others can keep older people active and connected, and they provide a feeling of respect that is easy to lose after retirement. Elena thought how unfortunate it was that so many societies retire people precisely when they are most capable of passing on what they know.

Every day at noon, Pavel and Nina sat together on the same bench in the Market square and ate their sandwiches slowly, talking and watching the town pass by. Neither of them was in any hurry, Elena noticed, and neither of them looked at a phone, since the conversation was the point of the meal. It was a daily appointment, and it was a habit with the strength of a sacred rule.

That night Elena wrote that the best evidence shows patterns and not single causes, and that real lives are complicated, with the habits that matter woven together like threads in a single cloth. It is tempting to pull out one thread and call it the secret, she wrote, but it is the whole cloth that keeps a person warm. She read the sentence twice and decided that it was true enough to keep.

Back in her flat in the city, Elena worked late at the desk, a half-eaten sandwich going stale beside her laptop, and for the first time she looked at her own habits as if they belonged to a stranger. Long hours of sitting, rushed lunches and late nights were exactly the opposite of everything she had been writing in her notebook about Nina. She put down her pen and felt rather foolish, like a doctor who has been caught smoking behind the surgery.

Elena counted the hours she spent sitting on an ordinary weekday, and the total was a shock. At the desk, on the train and in front of the television in the evening, she spent nearly all of her waking hours in a chair, with only the walk to the kettle to break them up. Her grandmother, she suspected, would have found the figure quite unbelievable, and might well have asked how anyone found time to get tired.

Elena ate her lunch alone at her desk in about ten minutes, answering messages with one hand, while Nina's midday meal lasted an hour and included soup, bread, vegetables and conversation. The contrast made Elena wince, and she wondered when she had decided that eating was an interruption of work and not part of living. It was an uncomfortable question for a person who prided herself on careful thinking.

Elena, who usually went to bed well after one o'clock with her phone glowing in her hand, woke each morning more tired than she had been the night before. She knew perfectly well from her own reading that regular late nights are not good for anyone, and the knowledge gave her no pleasure at all. It is one thing to understand evidence, she thought, and quite another to apply it.

Elena's mother Iris telephoned that evening, and her voice betrayed the worry that she usually concealed whenever the subject of Nina's age came up. She asked what Elena had discovered, and it was clear that she wanted two quite different things at once, which were an answer and a promise. Elena could give her the first, but she knew that she could not honestly give her the second.

After the call, Elena was seized by a reforming zeal and began to turn her notes into a list of rules, and within an hour the list had grown to forty items. She resolved to follow every one of them starting the next morning, from the extra walks and the new breakfast to the early nights and the daily call to a friend. It was a plan with all the realism of a New Year's resolution, and it was destined to meet the same fate by the following Friday.

On Sunday Elena showed the list of forty rules to her grandmother, and Nina laughed until she had to wipe her eyes with the corner of her apron. She told her granddaughter that she had never followed a list of rules in her entire life, and that she would not have lived long if she had tried. Elena felt somewhat deflated, and also a good deal relieved, as though a heavy rucksack had been taken from her shoulders.

Elena began to understand that copying another person's habits wholesale was not the answer, since cultures, bodies and circumstances differ so much from one life to another. A routine that suits an elderly woman in a hill town may not suit a young analyst in a big city, and in any case a list of forty rules tends to be abandoned within a week. What was needed, she saw, was something far smaller and far more realistic, a change that she could actually carry out on an ordinary Tuesday.

Elena chose just one small change to begin with, which was to leave her desk every day at lunchtime and walk for twenty minutes, with a colleague if she could persuade one to come. Small changes that fit into an existing day tend to survive, she had read, and they are most likely to last when the environment makes them easy, such as a walkable street near the office. She wrote the plan on a small card, put it above her desk where she could not avoid it, and felt unreasonably pleased with so modest a start.

On the phone that evening, Theo asked his aunt in his most serious voice whether she would live to be ninety, like his great-grandmother. Elena swallowed, smiled at the empty room, and answered that she hoped so with all her heart, and that she was going to try to enjoy every one of the years on the way there. It was the most honest answer that she could give, and it satisfied him completely.

In the corner shop, a magazine on the rack proclaimed in large letters that it had discovered the secret of a long life, and the article beneath described the daily habits of one very old man. Elena read the small print and found that the whole story rested on a single person's memory of what he had eaten, which is a flimsy foundation for a general rule. Newspaper stories of this kind, she wrote in the notebook, are often misleading, because one person's habits seldom explain the length of his life.

Pavel told Elena about his cousin Karl, who had smoked all his life and still lived to the age of ninety-five, and he seemed to think that this proved something. Elena explained gently that it proved only that Karl was lucky, since we rarely hear the stories of the many smokers who died younger, and the survivors are always the ones who tell the tale. This is called survivorship bias, she said, and it makes every story of an old rebel sound more convincing than the evidence deserves.

Many things in a life go together, Elena explained, such as wealth, schooling, safe work and good health, and so a link in the data does not prove that one thing causes another. Ice-cream sales and sunburn rise together every summer, she said, but ice cream does not cause sunburn, and the warm weather is the hidden cause behind both. She drew the seesaw on a napkin so that Theo could follow the argument.

Researchers call the hidden third factor a confounder, Elena explained, and it is the great enemy of nutritional science. In some old studies of alcohol, for example, the people who drank a little wine were also richer, better educated and healthier for many other reasons, and the wine took the credit that belonged to the money. It is the job of a careful scientist to hunt down such hidden causes.

Sometimes, Elena went on, the cause runs in the opposite direction from the one that people suppose. People who are already ill may cut down on drinking, exercise or work, and the resulting data can make the habit look more harmful, or more beneficial, than it really is, which is known as reverse causation. It means that every claim needs to be asked which came first, the habit or the illness.

The strongest evidence of cause comes from randomised trials, in which people are assigned by chance to one group or another, so that hidden factors are spread evenly between them. Such trials are hard to run for habits that last a lifetime, however, and nobody can ask a thousand people to smoke or exercise for fifty years, so most research on long life depends on observation. That is why careful scientists say that two things are linked, and are slow to say that one has caused the other.

Elena made a short checklist for reading any headline about health, which she stuck to the inside cover of the notebook. Who was studied, how many people were there, for how long, compared with whom, and how large was the difference in the end? A story that cannot answer these questions, she decided, belongs in the same drawer as the horoscopes.

A headline that announces that something doubles your risk can sound terrifying, but Elena showed her grandmother that the ratio is only half of the story. If the risk was very small to begin with, doubling it may still leave it small in real terms, while a modest increase in a very common risk can affect many thousands of people. Always ask for the absolute figure, she said, as well as the relative one.

A single study rarely settles anything, Elena explained, because it might be small, or unusual, or simply mistaken, and the same question must be asked again by other people in other places. When many studies and careful reviews point the same way, the case becomes far stronger, and good science changes its mind whenever the evidence demands it, as it did over alcohol. Changing one's mind, she said, is not a weakness of science but its greatest strength.

Elena decided to mark every claim in her notebook with a small traffic light, green for strong evidence, amber for mixed and red for weak, so that no reader could mistake a hunch for a fact. Nina leafed through the pages, saw how many amber lights there were, and said that she approved wholeheartedly, since honesty is rarely green. The notebook, which had begun as a list of facts, was becoming something more careful and more truthful.

To weigh the part played by inheritance, Elena turned to studies of twins, who share their genes, their birthdays and often their upbringing. These studies suggest that genes explain perhaps a fifth to a third of the differences in lifespan between people, although some newer estimates are lower, and scientists are still debating the exact figure. The conclusion was the same either way, which was that most of the story lies outside our genes.

Elena took care to explain that a figure for heritability describes the differences within a group of people at one time and place, and does not tell us how much of any life is fixed by genes. The figure itself can change from one country to another and from one century to the next, and it is a poor guide to personal destiny. It is, in short, a statement about populations and about averages, and not in any sense a prophecy about a particular man or woman.

Studies of centenarian families have found that their brothers and sisters tend to live longer than average, which suggests that long life does run partly in families. Elena cautioned, however, that families also share habits, kitchens, neighbourhoods and incomes, so the family effect is not all about genes, and no single gene has been shown to be a magic key. Long life is clearly a family inheritance in more than one sense, since it passes down habits and kitchens as well as genes.

Nina spoke quietly about her own parents, saying that her mother had lived to the age of eighty-eight, but that her father had died at fifty-one in an accident at work. One had a long life and the other a short one, she said, and neither had made a mistake that anybody could point to, which was why she had never believed that health was only a matter of virtue. Luck, she said, comes first and last, and everything that people do falls somewhere in between.

Nobody controls everything, Elena wrote, and genes, health care and plain chance all play a part in the length of a life. Good habits improve the odds, much as a careful driver improves the odds of a safe journey, but they cannot promise a long life, and there is no reason to look down on those who are unlucky. It was the most honest sentence that she had written so far, and it felt rather good to write.

Not everyone, Elena reminded herself, is free to choose a healthy way of living, since work, income and housing limit the options of millions of people. Safe streets, clean air, good health care and fair incomes therefore matter for whole communities, and it would be unkind to tell people to simply live better when the means to do so are out of their reach. Advice about habits, she wrote, should always come with a question about what is possible.

Habits changed even in middle age can still make a difference, and the clearest example is smoking, since research shows that people who give it up can regain many of the years that they might have lost. The earlier a person stops, the greater the gain, but the benefits begin soon after quitting and continue for years, and nobody should believe that it is too late. Tomas, who had given up smoking at sixty, nodded gravely and patted his chest.

Muscle strength in later life, Elena found, is linked with longer life and with the ability to remain independent, and weak grip and weak legs are warning signs in many studies. Small trials have shown that strength training can make even people in their nineties stronger, a result that surprised many doctors when it was first reported, and it supports the idea that the body can respond at any age. Nina, who was ninety, flexed an arm with great solemnity to see what would happen, and the family agreed that the result was impressive.

The real hope of health researchers, Elena wrote, is not to stretch the very end of life but to keep people well for as long as possible and to shorten the period of illness that comes before the end. This is sometimes called healthy ageing, and it is a hope that Nina said she shared, since few people would choose to add years of weakness to the ones that they already have. It was her own aim, set out on the first page of the project.

Nina said that she had never decided to be ninety but had simply kept going, one day at a time, and had enjoyed most of them. Elena realised that this humility about luck was itself a part of the answer, because it allowed Nina to enjoy her good fortune without claiming that she had earned it. It was, she thought, a rather wise and graceful way to hold a long life, lightly and with thanks, like a cup of tea that somebody else has made.

At last Elena asked the question that everybody asks the very old, which was for her grandmother's secret. Nina laughed so hard that she had to put down her teacup, and said that it was a little of everything and not worrying too much about any of it. A girl as clever as Elena, she added, ought to know that there is no secret at all, and that anybody who sells one is selling something else, so Elena wrote the answer down word for word.

Elena gathered her notes and distilled them into five themes, which she wrote on a card with a small picture beside each one. They were to move naturally, eat mostly plants, sleep enough, keep close people and have a reason to get up, and she was struck by how ordinary and how reasonable they looked. There was nothing exotic in the list, nothing to buy and nothing to be ashamed of.

Elena added that the five themes do not float in empty air, but sit inside a place, with its clean water, safe streets, local clinic and friendly shops. The place and the care, she wrote, matter as much as the habits and perhaps more, because they make good habits easy and bad ones less likely, and they work on everyone at once. It was the missing piece of her toast, and when she placed it in the sentence she was drafting, it fitted so well that she smiled.

Elena asked whether her grandmother followed the five themes on purpose, and Nina frowned, thought about it, and said that she did not. They simply fitted her life as it had grown up around her, she said, and she would not have known how to live in any other way, and that was probably the point. Habits that fit are easier to keep than habits that are chosen from a list.

Elena decided that the honest message for her toast would be that good habits improve the odds but promise nothing at all. Nobody should be told that a long life is simply a reward for good behaviour, she thought, nor that a short life is a punishment, and any story that says otherwise is both false and cruel. She tore up an earlier draft that had sounded rather too much like a sermon.

Theo made his own version of the five themes with crayons, in which Nina stood in the middle with a very large smile and a very small basket. Around her he drew figures walking, eating beans, sleeping in beds, playing with friends and bouncing out of bed in the morning with a smile. Elena stuck the drawing in her notebook, where it immediately became the best page in the book.

At Sunday dinner Elena reported her findings to the family, with her mother Iris and her brother Marek listening across the table and Theo drawing under it. She kept it simple, and she was careful to say which of the findings were strong, which were mixed and which were nothing more than interesting guesses, which was a respectful way to speak to people she loved. Marek, an engineer who distrusted anything that was not measured, asked three good questions and received three honest answers.

Iris admitted quietly that she was afraid of losing her mother one day, and the table fell silent for a moment. Elena took her hand and said honestly that nobody could promise anything, and that the research could not predict a single person's future, but that they could certainly spend the time that they had well. Nina, from the other end of the table, said that she was sitting right there and wished to be consulted.

The days before the party disappeared into baking, ironing and counting chairs, and Pavel arrived with a wooden box of his best tomatoes, polished like jewels. Nina nevertheless insisted that on the morning of her birthday she would walk to the market herself, as she had on every other morning, and nobody dared to argue with her. It was a small act of independence, and everybody understood its meaning without a word of discussion, including Pavel, who promised to save her the best apples.

On the night before the party, Elena wrote her toast by lamplight at her grandmother's kitchen table, crossing out one line after another until what remained was short and true. She closed her laptop at a sensible hour for once, brushed her teeth and went to bed early, since she had no wish to enjoy the party half asleep. Her list of forty rules would have been proud, and her grandmother would have laughed.

On the morning of the party, Nina put on her best dress and walked up the hill to the Market square with her basket, exactly as she did on every other morning. Elena walked beside her and found, with a pleasant shock, that she was a little less out of breath than she had been three weeks earlier. Nina bought a bag of apples, argued with Pavel about the price, and went home satisfied.

By noon the guests began to arrive at Nina's front gate with presents, flowers and balloons, and the narrow street outside the blue door filled with the noise of a family reunion. Four generations were present, from Nina herself down to Theo, and the old house, which had held so many parties in its sixty years, seemed to stretch itself to make room. Even the old tabby cat from next door had put on a respectable expression and settled on the wall to supervise the whole arrangement.

Pavel arrived with a crate of tomatoes and a handwritten card that wished his oldest customer many more years of arguing, and Rosa, Tomas and Hana followed close behind with a brand new deck of playing cards. They presented it to Nina with great solemnity and a warning that this time somebody would learn the rules. The whole company laughed loudly, since everyone knew perfectly well that nobody ever would, least of all the person who had bought the cards.

The cake appeared at last, carried by Marek with an expression of anxious concentration, and on top of it burned ninety small candles that threw a warm light over the faces of the guests. Theo counted them aloud, one by one, with his finger hovering over the flames, and for the first time that month he did not lose his place. When he reached ninety, the whole garden applauded him instead of Nina, who clapped louder than anyone and declared that the count was correct.

Nina drew a deep breath and blew out the candles in three determined puffs, while Theo and several of the other children helped with the last stubborn ones. When Theo asked her what she had wished for, she told him that the answer was a secret, then relented, and said that she had wished only for another good morning tomorrow. It was exactly what Elena would have expected, and it made her eyes sting.

The long lunch was simple and generous, with soup, fresh bread, vegetables from Pavel's stall, fish for the grown-ups and a great deal of conversation that rose and fell around the table. Nina ate her slice of cake with enjoyment and without any trace of guilt, and Elena, who had spent three weeks reading about food, found that she was simply glad to be eating it with the people she loved. The best evidence, she thought, was simply passing the salt along a table of people who had known one another for years.

Elena rose, raised her glass of water and told the guests that she had spent three weeks looking for the secret of a long life and had found something better and humbler. A long life, she said, is partly luck, partly place and partly habit, and the true aim is not only to add years to life but to add life to the years that we are given. The garden was silent for a moment, as if everyone were turning the sentence over, and then it broke into cheers and clinking glasses.

Nina rose, supporting herself with one hand on the table, and told her guests that she would not make a speech, which was a promise that she broke in the next sentence. She said that she would do it all again, mostly in the same way, and that if there was one thing she would change it would be to telephone her friends more often and to worry a good deal less. Then she sat down with great dignity to a storm of applause, and asked someone to pass her the cake.

As the last guests departed, Nina took Theo's hand and walked slowly with him through the Market square in the long evening light, past Pavel's folded stall and the baker's closed door. Elena watched them from the corner, and thought that the best evidence of a good life was not a number or a chart but a perfectly ordinary good day, with a small boy beside you. She did not write that in the notebook, because she did not need to.

Elena closed her notebook on the bench in the setting sun, glad that she had spent these weeks learning about the people who live long and the places that help them. This book has offered only general information, and it is not medical advice, so it cannot replace a conversation with a doctor who knows your own health and history. If you want to live well for a long time, start somewhere small, and perhaps start with a walk.
